# Assignment


<!-- WARNING: THIS FILE WAS AUTOGENERATED! DO NOT EDIT! -->

`←` assigns the value to its right to the target, the run just before
it. Besides plain names, a target can be a selection, a dot path, a
subscript or a list of names. With a function just before `←`, as in
`x+←1`, the assignment is modified. For the exact rules, see
[Assign](glyphs/assign.qmd) and [Syntax](syntax.qmd#assignment).

## Plain assignment

`x←Y` binds `x` to `Y` and returns `Y` without displaying it:

``` bpl
x←3
x+2
```

    5

A value can be a function, such as `+/`:

``` bpl
sum←+/
sum 1 2 3
```

    6

Assignments chain:

``` bpl
a←b←3
a+b
```

    6

Put independent assignments on separate lines or between `⋄`, because
`←` takes everything to its right:

``` bpl
p←1 q←2
p
```

    1 2

The name `_` discards a value. `_←Y` evaluates `Y` and keeps nothing.

## Modified assignment

`x f←Y` sets `x` to `x f Y`:

``` bpl
x+←3
x
```

    6

Any function works, such as `,` to append:

``` bpl
s←"abc"
s,←"d"
s
```

    abcd

A named function goes in parentheses, as `x(f)←Y`. In `x f←Y`, the
target would be `f`:

``` bpl
f←×
x(f)←4
x
```

    24

With nothing after the arrow, modified assignment applies the function
to the target alone. `x⌽←` sets `x` to `⌽x`:

``` bpl
x←1 2 3
x⌽←
x
```

    3 2 1

## Assigning to part of an array

A [subscript](scripts.ipynb#subscripts) target replaces one literal
position:

``` bpl
v←1 2 3
v₁←9
v
```

    1 9 3

Dot brackets name any positions, in plain or modified assignment:

``` bpl
v.[[0 2]]+←10
v
```

    11 9 13

Any other selection goes in parentheses, with a function that only
selects or rearranges, as for structural [Under](glyphs/under.qmd):

``` bpl
(2↑v)←8 9
v
```

    8 9 13

The selection can apply a function with rank. `0⌷⍤1` selects the first
item of each row:

``` bpl
M←[1 2
   3 4]
(0⌷⍤1 M)←9
M
```

    9 2
    9 4

A dot path writes a field of a record:

``` bpl
T←["n":1]
T.n+←1
T.n
```

    2

A plain assignment to a dot path creates any missing records along the
path:

``` bpl
T.addr.city←"SF"
T
```

    ["n":2 "addr":["city":"SF"]]

A subscript can follow a dot path:

``` bpl
T.a←1 2
T.a₁←7
T.a
```

    1 7

## Destructuring

A list of names in brackets destructures a value by position:

``` bpl
[a b]←10 20
a+b
```

    30

Each name takes one major cell of a higher-rank value, such as one row
of a matrix:

``` bpl
[top bottom]←2 3⍴⍳6
bottom
```

    3 4 5

A single value goes to every name:

``` bpl
[c d]←5
c d
```

    5 5

A nested list of names destructures a nested value:

``` bpl
[e [g h]]←[1 [2 3]]
h
```

    3

Modified assignment works on a list of names too:

``` bpl
[a b]+←10
a b
```

    20 30

Inside brackets, every name is a target, even one that holds a function,
such as `f`:

``` bpl
[f n]←1 2
f
```

    1

When the leading axis has a key on every position, each name takes the
item, or the major cell, with its key:

``` bpl
[b a]←["a":1 "b":2 "c":3]
a b
```

    1 2

A program takes names from a [module](modules.qmd) this way, as in
`[disp]←•load "lib/array.bpl"`.

## Names inside dfns

Inside a dfn, plain assignment makes a local name:

``` bpl
total←0
set←{total←⍵ ⋄ total}
_←set 5
total
```

    0

Modified and selective assignment update the nearest existing binding,
even outside the dfn:

``` bpl
add←{total+←⍵ ⋄ total}
_←add 5
total
```

    5

Arrays have value semantics, as numbers do:

``` bpl
u←1 2
w←u
u₀←9
w
```

    1 2
